# Lofoten Notes

## Overview

A week in the Lofoten islands in July 2025, in a rented car from the airport at Leknes and a rorbu cabin on stilts over the water. The islands are steep and narrow, the road runs along the shore with mountains on one side and the sea on the other, and every village sits at the end of a short detour. I came for the light and stayed for the walking. The weather changed on the hour, and I learned to take the sun when it came and not wait for a clear day.

The cabins are the old fishermen's huts, painted red or ochre, with two rooms and a small kitchen, and mine cost 180 EUR a night in high season. Cod hung on wooden frames to dry along the fences, and the smell of it carried across the harbour. I drove about 700 km over the week, never more than an hour and a half in one stretch, and the distances were short enough that I could change plans at lunchtime. The light never fully went, and I understood why people set alarms to photograph the middle of the night. The cod drying on the frames is the industry the islands were built on, and it is still working, not a display. The beaches at the southern end are white sand and turquoise water that looks Mediterranean until you put a hand in it. I kept a cooler bag in the car for the supermarket runs, because the nearest big shop was twenty minutes from the cabin.

## Notes

I arrived on the last ferry of the evening, the boat from Bodø that takes about three and a half hours and threads between islands before docking at Moskenes well after the sun had stopped setting. The crossing was calm but cold on deck, and I stood at the rail most of the way watching the mountains grow out of the sea. I had a cabin on the ferry for the first hour and spent the rest on my feet. By the time I drove off the ramp, collected the car from the lot and found the rorbu, it was close to midnight and still light enough to read a map outside. That first night set the pattern: no darkness to tell me to sleep, and a sky that stayed a soft grey-blue until the small hours.

The cabin itself was small and warm, two rooms, a kitchen with a two-ring hob, a shower the size of a cupboard and a porch over the water where I ate most of my meals. The stove kept the rooms dry, which mattered, because the wind off the fjord carries a damp that gets into everything left outside. I hung my walking clothes on the porch rail and they dried in the constant light within an hour.

The wind is the thing I underestimated. It blows steadily down the fjords and turns a warm afternoon cold in minutes, and it will take a door out of your hand or a plate off a table. I kept a shell jacket on the hook by the door and wore it every single day, even when the sky looked kind. Midges came out in the still evenings near the grass and the bog, and I used a head net once and a repellent the rest of the time. The midges were worse inland by the lakes than anywhere on the coast, and worst of all on a windless evening.

Supermarkets in Reine open late on weekdays and close early at the weekend, and by Sunday evening the shelves were thin. I bought what I needed on the Saturday morning, and the little shop shut at six. Fuel stations are mostly unmanned, and the pumps take a card at any hour, so I never had trouble filling up, though the shop attached to one closed at eight and the one on the main road closed at nine. I never ran the tank below a quarter, because the villages are far apart.

The road tunnels are unlit in places or dimly lit, and one of them is long enough that the lights seem to go on for ever. They are narrow and single-lane in the oldest sections, and you yield to oncoming traffic at the passing bays. I drove them slowly the first time and in the middle of the lane the second.

The hike up Reinebringen is the walk everyone does, up a long flight of stone steps laid by Sherpas, and it takes about an hour at a steady pace. The steps are steep and there is no rail, and I took it slowly with two stops. The view from the top over the village and the fjord is the picture you have seen, and it earns every step. I went up in the late evening when the crowds had thinned.

There is no launderette in most villages, and I washed by hand in the cabin sink and dried on the porch in the light. What closed on a Sunday surprised me: the small supermarkets, the museum, and the one café in the village. The petrol station shop stayed open. Driving distances are short in kilometres but slow in time, because the road bends and climbs, so a village twenty minutes away on paper can take forty in practice. I learned to add half again to any estimate. The weather changed hourly, and I stopped trusting the morning sky by the second day. The best walks are signposted but poorly marked on the ground, and I took a paper map and a compass on the two longer routes, because the phone lost signal in the valleys. The fishing villages are quiet in the middle of the day and busy around the evening ferry, and the harbour at Å is the end of the road and worth the drive. I ate fresh fish most nights, bought from a shop counter in one village and cooked simply in the cabin. The shower was small and the hot water was limited, so I learned to be quick. Bikes are for hire in several villages and the flatter stretches along the shore are easy, though the wind makes the return harder than the outbound leg. I paid for the car park at Reinebringen with a phone app, which is the pattern for most of the trailheads. The roads are two lanes and well kept, but a motorhome or a truck on a blind bend leaves little room, so I kept to the speed limit and pulled in when a queue built behind me. The midges were at their worst on the still evenings near the freshwater lakes and disappeared entirely on the coast when the wind got up, which is most of the time. I would bring a better map, a warmer hat, a second pair of gloves and a proper head torch, and I would book the rorbu earlier than I did. A week is the right length; longer and I would have started to hunger for a city.

## Costs

The rorbu was the big line, 180 EUR a night for seven nights, which came to 1260 EUR, and I would pay it again for the porch over the water. The car rental was 420 EUR for the week with unlimited kilometres, and fuel came to about 90 EUR for the 700 km, the roads being steady rather than fast. The ferry from Bodø was 30 EUR for a foot passenger and the car went separately on an earlier sailing.

Food I mostly cooked, about 30 EUR a day from the supermarket, with two meals out at roughly 45 EUR each. The total for the week landed near 1600 EUR, a little under the figure I had in my head, and the ferry and the fuel together cost less than the cabin alone. I would go again in the same month and book the cabin earlier, because the good ones go a year ahead. Parking at the trailheads cost a few euros by app, and the ferries inside the islands were free after the main crossing. I would plan the same budget again and add a little for the boat trips and the museum entries I skipped, since the sea safari alone was 90 EUR.
